sandhi.rule: एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि (6.1.132); अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101)
sandhi.note: सः drops its visarga before a consonant. स्वयम् is only written together with एव; एव + अधितिष्ठति: a + a → ā.

samasa.vigraha: सूर्यश्च इन्द्रश्च अग्निश्च अनिलश्च इन्दुश्च, तेषाम्
samasa.literal: of Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon
samasa.sense: the great gods whose functions keep the world running

morph.note: Present of अधि + √स्था, ‘to stand over, occupy’. With अधि the place one occupies is the object, in the accusative (अधिकारान्). The present tense makes the gods’ complaint vivid: he holds the posts now.
अधिकार (अधि + √कृ + घञ्) is ‘authority, office, function’: the share of the world’s working that belongs to each god.

mantras.anvaya: सः (महिषः) स्वयम् एव सूर्येन्द्राग्न्यनिलेन्दूनां यमस्य वरुणस्य च अन्येषां च अधिकारान् अधितिष्ठति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject, an emphatic स्वयम् एव, a long genitive list dependent on अधिकारान्, and the verb.
mantras.lit: Of the Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon, of Yama and Varuṇa, and of the others, the offices he himself alone occupies.
mantras.tr: He has seized for himself the offices of the Sun, Indra, Fire, Wind and Moon, of Yama and Varuṇa, and of the other gods besides.
mantras.tr_note: tr puts the verb first and renders the present ‘occupies’ as ‘has seized’, which is its sense here.

comm.t: The gods’ speech to Śiva and Viṣṇu begins here (2.6–8). Mahiṣa has not only taken Indra’s throne (2.3); he has taken over every god’s function himself.

The list reads as an inventory of the cosmos: light (Sun), rule (Indra), sacrifice (Agni), breath (Wind), the waters (Varuṇa), death (Yama), the moon. When one asura holds them all, the order of the world is in the hands of its enemy. The Goddess who answers this will receive gifts from these very gods (2.20–31).

The prefix दुस् ‘bad’ becomes दुर् before the vowel ā.

samasa.sense: the gods in all their companies

morph.note: Past passive participle of निर् + आ + √कृ ‘to put away, repudiate’: ‘cast out’. Its agent stands in the instrumental, तेन … महिषेण दुरात्मना.
Locative of the root-noun भू ‘earth’: before vowel endings ū becomes uv (भुवि, भुवः).

mantras.anvaya: तेन दुरात्मना महिषेण स्वर्गात् निराकृताः सर्वे देवगणाः भुवि मर्त्याः यथा विचरन्ति।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (सर्वे देवगणाः) with a participial phrase (स्वर्गात् निराकृताः, agent तेन … महिषेण दुरात्मना), then the verb with a comparison (मर्त्याः यथा).
mantras.lit: Driven out of heaven by him, by the evil-minded Mahiṣa, all the hosts of gods wander on the earth like mortals.
mantras.tr: Cast out of heaven by that wicked Mahiṣa, all the gods now wander the earth like mortal men.

comm.t: The second part of the complaint: the gods are exiles, wandering the earth like humans. The gods’ condition now matches Suratha’s, who also lost his kingdom and wandered alone (1.6–11).
A modern reading: the text lets even the gods lose their place. Being dispossessed is not a mark of unworthiness here; it is the condition from which help is sought.

Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra. The same happens in कथितं सर्वम्.
-aḥ before the voiced v becomes -o; the visarga of वधः before t becomes s.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (outer), containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (अमरारि)
samasa.literal: the doing of the enemy of the deathless

morph.note: The enclitic वः stands for युष्मद् in the accusative, dative or genitive plural. The first वः goes with कथितम् (‘told to you’); the second is the person whose shelter is sought. The gods address two (Śiva and Viṣṇu, the dual of 2.4) in the plural; this is either the plural of respect or includes Brahmā, who leads them.
Past participle of प्र + √पद् with active sense (a verb of motion): ‘having approached’. शरणं प्रपद् is the fixed idiom ‘to go to (someone) for refuge’, with the person in the accusative.
Passive imperative (third person): ‘let his death be thought out’. A polite way to put a request to superiors.

mantras.anvaya: एतत् सर्वम् अमरारिविचेष्टितं वः कथितम्। वः शरणं प्रपन्नाः स्मः। तस्य वधः विचिन्त्यताम्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three short clauses: a passive statement (कथितम्), an active one (प्रपन्नाः स्मः) and a passive request (विचिन्त्यताम्).
mantras.lit: This, all the doings of the enemy of the immortals, has been told to you. We have come to you for refuge; let his killing be devised.
mantras.tr: We have told you all that the enemy of the gods has done. We have come to you for refuge: find a way to destroy him.
mantras.tr_note: tr turns the two passives into active English.

comm.t: The gods end their report and ask for help: they take refuge with the high gods and ask them to plan Mahiṣa’s death. They do not ask the gods to fight; they ask them to think (विचिन्त्यताम्). What answers is not a plan but anger, and from the anger the Goddess comes (2.9–13).
शरणं प्रपद् ‘to go for refuge’ is the language of surrender (prapatti). The same request, made to the Goddess herself, runs through the gods’ hymns in chapters 4, 5 and 11.

words.en: both with faces twisted by frowning brows
words.g: m. nom. dual; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies मधुसूदनः and शम्भुः together

sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra; likewise देवानां वचांसि and कोपं शम्भुः.
Visarga before c becomes s, and s next to c becomes ś.

samasa.sense: Viṣṇu, named for his victory in the first carita (1.92–103)

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi containing a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa (भ्रुकुटीकुटिल: भ्रुकुट्या कुटिलम्)
samasa.literal: the two whose faces are crooked with frowning

morph.note: Perfect of √कृ (reduplicated च-कार). कोपं चकार ‘made anger’ is the idiom for ‘grew angry’. The verb is singular with two subjects joined by च: it agrees with the nearer subject, while the adjective भ्रुकुटीकुटिलाननौ is dual and covers both.
Absolutive of नि + √शम्, ‘having perceived, heard’ (compare निशामय in 1.2, from the causative of the same root).

mantras.anvaya: इत्थं देवानां वचांसि निशम्य मधुसूदनः शम्भुः च भ्रुकुटीकुटिलाननौ (सन्तौ) कोपं चकार।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive phrase (इत्थं … निशम्य), two subjects with one dual adjective, and the verb with its object.
mantras.lit: Having heard thus the words of the gods, Madhusūdana grew angry, and Śambhu, both with faces twisted by frowning brows.
mantras.tr: Hearing the gods speak in this way, Viṣṇu and Śiva grew angry, their faces dark with frowning brows.
mantras.tr_note: tr uses the names Viṣṇu and Śiva for Madhusūdana and Śambhu.

comm.t: The response to the gods’ appeal is anger, not counsel. Viṣṇu is called Madhusūdana, a reminder of his victory over Madhu in the first carita, a victory won only when the Goddess released him from sleep.

Anger is the starting point of the whole manifestation that follows: the tejas comes from the angered faces (2.10). The tradition reads the Goddess of this carita, who presides over action and battle, as coming out of this righteous wrath.

sandhi.note: -aḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, a + u → o, and the following a is elided (avagraha).
-aḥ before the voiced v becomes -o; likewise तेजो ब्रह्मणः.
The s of the prefix निस् becomes ś next to c.

morph.note: Perfect of निस् + √क्रम्: reduplicated च-क्राम (k → c in the reduplication). ‘Stepped out, issued forth’, of the tejas leaving the face.
The verse uses ततः twice. The first is ‘then’; the second, after वदनात्, is best taken in its ablative sense, ‘from there’, reinforcing the source. See Uncertain.
Genitive of चक्रिन् ‘one who has the discus’: the in-stem with the possessive taddhita -इन्.

mantras.anvaya: ततः अतिकोपपूर्णस्य चक्रिणः वदनात् ततः ब्रह्मणः शंकरस्य च (वदनात्) महत् तेजः निश्चक्राम।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject महत् तेजः and the verb निश्चक्राम, with the source in the ablative (वदनात्) and three possessors in the genitive.
mantras.lit: Then, from the face of the discus-bearer, filled with intense anger, from there, came forth a great radiance, and from Brahmā and Śaṅkara.
mantras.tr: Then from the face of Viṣṇu, the bearer of the discus, burning with anger, a great radiance came forth, and from the faces of Brahmā and Śiva as well.
mantras.tr_note: The second ततः is absorbed into ‘from’; ‘the faces’ is supplied for Brahmā and Śiva.

comm.t: The tejas of the three great gods comes first, out of their faces, in their anger. Viṣṇu is named first and his anger is stressed (अतिकोप).

Tejas is more than light: it is the fiery power and splendour that belongs to a god. The order in which the tejas comes out (Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Śiva, then the others) is matched later by the parts of the Goddess’s body formed from each (2.14–18).

flags.uncertain: The second ततः (end of the first line) is read as ‘from there’, reinforcing वदनात्. It can also be taken as a resumptive ‘then’, filling the line; the sense is the same.
